The embryonic development of Bactrocera oleae begins when a fertilised female deposits an egg within the mesocarp of an olive fruit, where each freshly laid ovum exhibits a wet weight of 0.01 grams [Ww0 = 0.01 grams], a modest initial mass that reflects the yolk-limited reserves of this tephritid species. Following oviposition, the embryo undergoes rapid organogenesis within the chorionate egg, and at a constant incubation temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], hatchling emergence from the egg occurs after an age at birth of approximately 2.7 days [ab = approximately 2.7 days]. This brief embryonic period is typical of many dacine fruit flies, allowing neonates to quickly access the nutrient-rich olive pulp. Once the first instar larva begins active feeding, it measures a body length of instar 1 of 0.39 centimeters , a value that represents the onset of an accelerating growth trajectory. The newly hatched larva immediately starts mining the fruit tissue, initiating the exotrophic transition that will sustain the rapid mass accumulation characteristic of the larval-juvenile phase.

During the larval feeding period, the insect passes through two additional instars before reaching the pre-pupal stage. The second instar, which follows the first moult, attains a body length of instar 2 of 0.54 centimeters , representing a substantial increase in linear dimensions compared to the earlier stage. By the end of the third and final larval instar, the larva reaches a body length of instar 3 of 0.7 centimeters , the maximum recorded size before the cessation of feeding and the onset of pupariation. This rapid increase in body length reflects the larva's ability to efficiently convert olive pulp into body tissue, with growth rates that are tightly coupled to the nutritional quality of the host fruit. The larval duration for the olive group, measured from eclosion to pupariation, was recorded as 13.0 days  at a stable rearing temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], providing a clear benchmark for the developmental schedule under controlled conditions.

At the moment of pupariation, the mature larva exhibits a length at pupation of 0.514 centimeters , a slight reduction from the maximum larval length that results from the contraction and hardening of the cuticle during the formation of the puparium. Concurrently, the wet weight at pupation was measured at 0.00668 grams  in individuals reared on the control food diet, indicating a considerable loss of water content as the larva transitions to the non-feeding pupal stage. The pupal duration under the same thermal regime of 26 °C [T = 26 °C] was determined to be 7.0 days , representing the time from the formation of the puparium to the emergence of the pharate adult. This relatively brief metamorphic interval is typical of tephritids adapted to the warm summer conditions of Mediterranean olive groves.

Upon eclosion from the puparium, the newly emerged adult fly, or imago, displays a length at emergence of 0.587 centimeters , a measurement that places it among the smaller-bodied members of the Bactrocera genus. The reproductive maturation of these adults is highly dependent on thermal conditions, with females reaching the reproductively viable organism stage after a relatively short interval. The ultimate reproduction rate for this species, defined as the maximum number of eggs laid per female per day, attains a value of 19.0 eggs per day [Ri = 19.0 eggs per day] under controlled conditions at 24 °C [T = 24 °C]. This elevated fecundity is a key life-history trait that allows B. oleae populations to increase rapidly when host fruits are abundant, and it substantially exceeds the rates reported for many other frugivorous tephritids of comparable adult body size.

Female imago longevity under standard laboratory conditions, recorded at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], reaches 98.2 days [am = 98.2 days] for individuals fed on the control diet, a lifespan that accommodates multiple successive oviposition bouts over the course of a single growing season. This extended reproductive window, combined with a high daily egg output, enables a single female to contribute significantly to the next generation under favorable environmental conditions. In comparison to congeneric species such as Bactrocera dorsalis, the lifespan of B. oleae females is notably longer, a difference that may reflect adaptations to the relatively predictable but seasonal availability of olive fruits. The interplay between temperature-dependent development and adult longevity is critical for predicting population dynamics in this economically important pest, underscoring the need for accurate thermal profiles in integrated pest management strategies.
